en.title: DC's Lanterns: The Manhunters' Messy Origin Explained
en.summary: The new DC series 'Lanterns' is diving deep into the convoluted history of the Manhunters, the robotic precursors to the Green Lantern Corps. Their origin story is far more complex than just killer androids.
en.body:
DC's **Lanterns** series is only two episodes in, but it's already proving that the universe of the Green Lantern Corps is far stranger and more convoluted than some might have anticipated. The show has started to explore the origins of the **Manhunters**, the ancient, unfeeling android enforcers created by the Guardians of the Universe long before the Green Lantern Corps. While the on-screen narrative presents them as the Lanterns' bitter, brutal enemies, their history within DC Comics lore is a tangled web of retcons and revisions, making them arguably the messiest antagonists in DC history.

Eons ago, the Maltusans, a hyper-advanced and immortal race, sought utopia. However, one of their scientists, **Krona**, dared to witness the dawn of creation, inadvertently introducing evil into the universe. Filled with regret, a faction of Maltusans became the **Guardians of the Universe**, dedicating themselves to enforcing justice and protecting life. Their initial attempt at achieving this was the creation of the **Manhunters**, sophisticated androids powered by the same emerald energy that would later fuel the Green Lanterns. These early enforcers were designed to be devoid of emotion, ensuring impartial justice. However, their programming and their masters' perceived leniency eventually led them to rebel, believing their own remorseless interpretation of justice was superior.

## The Guardians' Flawed First Attempt

The **Manhunters** represent a critical early failure in the Guardians' long and often morally ambiguous mission to police the cosmos. Created as the universe's first intergalactic police force, these androids were designed to operate without the emotional biases that the Guardians believed plagued organic life. Their mission was to impose order with absolute impartiality, a goal that, in practice, often translated to ruthless efficiency and a disregard for life. The inherent flaw in their design, or perhaps in the Guardians' understanding of justice, was that true impartiality can become cruelty when devoid of empathy. Their rebellion against the Guardians wasn't just a power grab; it was a philosophical schism, with the Manhunters believing their creators were too soft and that only absolute, unfeeling enforcement could truly bring order to the chaos of the universe. This fundamental conflict has made them recurring and deeply personal adversaries for the Green Lanterns, who embody the *ideal* of justice tempered by will and emotion.

## Why This Matters to Lanterns Fans

For dedicated fans of **Green Lantern** comics, the exploration of the **Manhunters**' complex, often contradictory history is a treasure trove. The show's willingness to delve into these deep cuts signals a commitment to the rich, sometimes messy, lore that makes the Green Lantern universe so unique. It also raises intriguing questions about how these various iterations of the Manhunters' origins will be integrated into the series. Will **John Stewart** and **Hal Jordan** grapple with the fact that the 'official' DC lore might differ from what other fans understand? This narrative approach allows the series to appeal to both long-time comic readers who know the intricate details and newer viewers who are just discovering the vastness of the GL mythology. The stakes are not just about defeating a robotic menace, but about understanding the very foundations of galactic justice and the Guardians' own complicated legacy.

## What's Next

As **Lanterns** continues its run, expect further revelations about the Manhunters' origins and their ongoing impact on the Green Lantern Corps. The series is poised to explore the philosophical divides that continue to plague the Guardians' grand experiment, promising more complex character interactions and universe-building.

We’re only two episodes in, and Lanterns has already had a lot more comic book weirdness than some detractors had guessed from the trailers. But when John Stewart asks Hal Jordan about Manhunters, Lanterns gets really weird. Most fans of Green Lantern comics know Manhunters as the killer androids created by the Guardians of the Universe before the Green Lantern Corps , unfeeling and brutal enforcers of justice who have become one of the Lanterns’ most bitter enemies. But behind the scenes, the Manhunters are some of the most convoluted characters in DC Comics history, the result of multiple retcons and revisions. So while John and Hal know Manhunters as killer robots, other DC Comics fans may think the Lanterns are talking about something else… and they may be correct. The Secret Origin of the Manhunters Here is the official DC lore about Manhunters: Eons ago, the citizens of the planet Maltus achieved perfect utopia and immortality, and devoted themselves to scientific research. However, one of their number, a scientist named Krona, went too far and found a way to witness the dawn of creation. Doing so introduced evil into the universe, filling the Maltusans with regret. As penance, a group of Maltusans became the Guardians of the Universe, and searched for a way to enforce justice and protect the innocent. One of their early experiments in this project was the creation of the Manhunters, androids infused with the same emerald energy that would later power the Green Lantern Corps. Initially, the Manhunters did their job well. But they grew dissatisfied with what they perceived as weakness in their masters and eventually rebelled, pursuing their idea of justice without remorse. When the Manhunters killed nearly everyone in Space Sector 666, the Guardians sent the androids into exile, spread across many planets, including Earth. The Manhunters disguised themselves as citizens on these planets and, on Earth, established a cult. The Manhunter Cult, led by a mustachioed man called the Grandmaster, would recruit humans of exceptional skill and send them on dangerous missions. The most famous example is Mark Shaw, who became an ally of Batman and the Justice League before leading the crime organization Leviathan. The Manhunters also prepared for the next step of human evolution by placing sleeper agents in the lives of prominent superheroes, replacing people like Commissioner James Gordon and Superman ‘s childhood pal Pete Ross with robot imposters in the much-reviled 1988 DC crossover Millennium . Despite their defeat in Millennium , the Manhunters regularly show up to hassle Green Lanterns, making them one of the franchise’s most reliable villains. But they didn’t start that way.
